abstract: Researchers at Lucid Motors and EYL Inc. published “From FIPS to FPGA with LLM Agents: Measuring What Tests and Reviews Miss in Post-Quantum Cryptographic Hardware.” Abstract “As LLM agents increasingly generate RTL alongside the tests and reviews that validate it, self-generated evidence is a weak foundation for trustworthy hardware. We present our seven-stage verification-gated workflow, evolved during a post-quantum design port, in which a gate counts only if shown able to fail on negative controls and fault mutants, and reviewer agents audit work before commit. We then audit this evidence with tool-selected netlist mutants, flaw replays, and formal checks. The flow ported an ML-KEM-768/ML-DSA-65 accelerator to a 300 MHz Zynq UltraScale+ key-custody card: all six operations are byte-exact on the board, and it passes all 85 interface-applicable NIST ACVP cases (of 285) and 484 ML-DSA known answers. However, passing module tests overstate the verification strength. Across three RTL modules, existing simulation gates kill only 76% of 399 tool-selected netlist mutants; specification-derived tests guided by the survivors raise the fresh-draw decapsulation kill rate from 48% to 74%. In pre-registered single-model replays on flaws invisible to known-answer tests, undirected whole-design review catches two verifier flaws in only 3/6 and 1/6 sessions, whereas module-scoped review catches every known flaw in all 54 sessions. Even scoped review detects planted key-custody flaws in only 3/20 sessions, whereas formal checks (one added for the replay) flag every one. In this study, trustworthy agentic hardware needed author-independent mutants for test gates, module-level scoping for LLM review, and formal checks for custody invariants.” Find the technical paper here . abstract: Plasma etching and deposition processes increasingly determine the manufacturability of advanced semiconductor devices, where smaller features, more complex geometries, stricter wafer-uniformity requirements, and new chemistries demand predictive control of ion fluxes at the wafer surface. Kinetic plasma simulation provides a physics-based route to this control by resolving sheath dynamics, ion-neutral transport, and ion angular and energy distributions that cannot be captured reliably with bulk fluid approximations alone. VSim Plasma applies Particle-in-Cell modeling with Monte Carlo collisions to compute self-consistent electromagnetic fields, charged-particle motion, collisions, and current deposition. Validation against inductively coupled plasma measurements shows strong agreement for electron temperature and plasma potential, reasonable density agreement, and consistent electron energy probability function behavior. Coupling plasma-derived ion angular and energy distributions into Victory Process enables feature-scale etch simulation, linking chamber conditions and waveform design to process variability and profile evolution. Read more here . [Download for PDF is here .] Fig. 1: Chamber-scale plasma simulation. Source: Silvaco The post Simulation of Plasma Chambers for Predictive Simulation of Semiconductor Manufacturing appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering .

abstract: Key Takeaways: AI can identify promising process conditions and recognize manufacturing problems, but those results still require physical validation before they can be trusted in production. Incomplete manufacturing data and uncertainty about downstream effects make it difficult to give AI systems authority over process adjustments. Greater manufacturing autonomy will require clear decision boundaries, failure containment, and ways to qualify models that change as they learn. Semiconductor manufacturing has always depended on engineers making decisions involving complex interactions among process parameters. An etch recipe, for example, may involve combinations of RF power, pressure, gas chemistry, temperature, and timing, each affecting multiple process characteristics. Changing one parameter might improve critical dimension control while creating problems elsewhere. But as devices and manufacturing processes become more complicated, the growing number of variables involved makes those decisions increasingly difficult. AI-driven manufacturing offers a way to manage some of that complexity, from finding better process conditions to identifying defects and responding to problems on the production line. abstract: Key T ake a ways: CPO and NPO require new approaches for connecting optical fibers to chip packages. Detachable connectors can simplify assembly, test, and replacement of optical components. Numerous bespoke designs exist today, but standardization hasn’t begun yet. As photonics shifts from pluggable optical transceivers toward near- and co-packaged optics (NPO, CPO), engineers are devising new ways to attach fibers to the photonics chips on a board. Several different designs exist today, but so far there is no common interface. With pluggable photonics, lasers and connections are attached at the server faceplate, with the board itself housing only electronic components. Yet long electrical connections to the faceplate mean higher power and longer latency. Fibers would need to move onto the interior of the board to solve that. That eliminates the need for pluggables, but it requires new solutions. “With the rapid growth of generative AI, AI data centers are required to process enormous volumes of data faster and more efficiently than ever before,” said Yoshimasa Bando, principal scientist at Mitsubishi Chemical . “To meet this demand, further improvements in communication speed and energy efficiency have become critical challenges.” The goal of CPO and NPO is to reduce reliance on long electrical connections. Long lines One reason for maintaining faceplate pluggables is that lasers are not always reliable. abstract: Key Takeaways: AI accelerators and GPUs consume thousands of amperes at increasingly low voltages, causing a shift to vertical power delivery that brings regulation closer to loads. Advances in integrated voltage regulators and passive components are enabling new power architectures. Power delivery is becoming a system-level co-design challenge, expanding simulation needs and the role of OSATs. Power delivery is now a significant performance limiter in data center chips. The demands of AI and high-performance computing chips running near 0.7 V for a 600W GPU are forcing current to rise to 1,000 amps and beyond, compounding resistive losses and voltage droop across the PDN. Multi-chiplet constructions only compound these issues by further increasing current density and signal congestion. To solve these challenges, designers are turning to vertical power delivery networks, where the voltage regulator modules are relocated much closer to the processors from their position on the device periphery — to the PCB landside (under the PCB), inside the accelerator package, or inside the silicon interposer. Together with the growing customization of AI accelerator modules, there are many approaches on offer with varying design and manufacturing complexity. The vertical PDN trend began nearly a decade ago with the integration of backside power delivery networks (BPDNs) on the wafer backside, enabling fine-tuned power delivery more directly to the transistors while reducing IR drop across the tens of interconnect levels on-chip. That approach is being extended with increasingly sophisticated on-die decoupling capacitors (DCaps) formed in deep trenches as part of the BPDN. Consumption-based pricing could reshape EDA business models, but trust and proprietary data remain obstacles. AI agents are emerging as a new category of reusable design capability, but with a twist. Rather than providing tightly defined design blocks, agents can be used to explore different options, integrate them, and use those changes to improve designs. At the leading edge, soft IP developers have been customizing their code for large customers for more than a decade to boost performance and/or reduce power. But that customization is typically narrow and costly, and optimizations for one design may not directly transfer to derivative chips — especially multi-die assemblies at the leading edge. Agents, in contrast, can be used to customize different functions with little or no human intervention, and they can self-optimize for different workloads and use cases, and some agents can even adjust for aging hardware. abstract: NVIDIA’s Ian Buck kicked off the company’s week at SC26 in Chicago on Monday with new tools for AI agents, software that can plan experiments, run code and check results on researchers’ own systems. In NVIDIA’s special address, Buck announced Nemotron for Science , the Rubin HPC GPU and an expanded Vera CPU platform for high-performance computing . He also detailed a new collaboration in quantum computing with IBM and Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory . “The frontier of computing and the new scientific stack is going to be simulation, as always, but combined with AI and the future of quantum,” said Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA. Buck opened the talk by looking back to his first public talk on CUDA, at an SC06 tutorial in Tampa, Florida, 20 years ago. NVIDIA now offers more than 1,000 CUDA-X libraries , he said. Open Models for Science Agents “[Agents] have been just a game changer in how we interface with our supercomputers, with our devices, our instruments and how we can do the research,” Buck said. Simulation remains the foundation of scientific computing, “which will always be on the top,” Buck said, with AI, quantum and now agents working alongside it. abstract: Researchers at Georgia Tech, NVIDIA Research , and Stanford University published “SlipStream: Enabling HBF for GPU Systems by Mitigating the Latency and SRAM Overheads.” Abstract Excerpt “Large language model (LLM) inference demands ever more memory capacity for larger models and batch sizes. High-Bandwidth Flash (HBF) replaces the DRAM dies of HBM with NAND flash and provides up to 16x the capacity at comparable read bandwidth. However, HBF can incur a read latency of nearly 20 μ s, 20x that of HBM, so on-demand HBF accesses slow inference by up to 12.8x. Conventional cache-line prefetchers require 20x more in-flight tracking state to cover this latency. Tensor-streaming designs, such as H3, follow virtual-address order as opposed to kernel-demand order, and therefore need hundreds of megabytes of buffering. We propose SlipStream, a software-hardware co-designed prefetcher that turns prefetching into a demand-paced producer-consumer pipeline. In software, SlipStream profiles the repeatable weight-page demand order of data-independent LLM kernels and inserts a staging warp that replays this order with non-blocking STAGE instructions. In hardware, the staging warp acts as the producer and the work warps as consumers. Our key insight is to retire each STAGE tracking entry only when demand first accesses the page, as opposed to when the page returns from HBF. Demand thus paces staging and bounds how far staging leads consumption. SlipStream tracks 4 KB pages instead of cache lines and allocates buffer slots only when pages return, which decouples the buffer size from outstanding traffic. abstract: We all know how important inspection is for advanced packaging. Not only are these processes critical for ensuring higher yield, but they’re also integral for maintaining device reliability. As the industry pushes for smaller features and tighter spacing, even the smallest defects can pose major challenges. For instance, delaminations and air gaps can be detrimental in a market that demands increasingly complex devices. Such defects will lead to electrical or mechanical failures down the road. One technology that’s mitigating these issues is acoustic micro imaging (AMI). AMI is a high-frequency ultrasound technology, and it’s being used by the industry as an inspection method. How AMI works At the core of AMI technology is a transducer, or a device that turns energy from one form to another. It starts with a pulse of electrical energy, then converts it to mechanical energy, or a high-frequency ultrasound wave. Because ultrasound doesn’t travel through air, this allows inspectors to obtain clear images of gaps and delaminations in the device that could otherwise be difficult to see. However, the transducers used for AMI are not all the same. Each transducer handles a specific frequency, and they’re chosen based on the sample that needs to be inspected. By moving the transducer across the sample, the inspector can generate multiple images that can then be analyzed by the AMI software. Through this analysis, the inspector can choose to accept or reject parts based on the number of defects the package is found to have. So, how do these defects typically present themselves? The biggest difference between ideal and defective samples is that some defective samples will have very clear air gaps. However, another common defect is thinning of the attach material on solder pads.…

abstract: Third public-beta release of NVIDIA ALCHEMI Toolkit. The headline is distillation : teacher scoring, offline and on-policy training loops that run data-parallel, and an acceptance evaluation suite. This release also adds enhanced sampling, batched minimum-energy paths, a generative model API, L-BFGS optimizers, and LoRA fine-tuning. Distillation Train a compact student potential against a larger teacher, from a fixed dataset or from the student's own trajectories. Teacher scoring and offline labeling — a TeacherScorer protocol and public TeacherSignal specs; built-in signals ( energy , forces , stress , atomic_energies , embeddings , hessian ) are requested by name. label_dataset persists the teacher fields to a resumable Zarr store. Offline strategy — DistillationStrategy trains a student against a "teacher" ; teacher signals arrive as teacher_* batch fields, so any built-in loss term distills by pointing its target_key at one. New AtomicEnergyMatchingLoss matches per-atom energy decompositions. On-policy segment loop — the student's own propagator generates frames, TeacherLabelHook attaches teacher_* fields, and a ReplayBuffer feeds exact reference/replay mixtures. Relaxation propagators are supported via fmax and a convergence hook. Opt-in settings cap trajectory length ( max_trajectory_steps , which recycles the seed pool) and freeze diverged frames ( quarantine_diverged ). Multi-GPU on-policy — data-parallel under a DDPHook : each rank labels its own shard with its own teacher replica. Embedding, Hessian, and Boltzmann objectives — three loss terms distill what no reference dataset carries: per-atom representations, Hessian-vector products, and Boltzmann relative entropy.
